title: Friction‐Corrected In‐Situ Viscosity Measurement in Material Extrusion: A Force‐Based Method Validated Against Capillary Rheometry Using Identical Nozzle Geometry
abstract: ABSTRACT The extrusion force in fused filament fabrication carries information about the melt state, but published force‐to‐viscosity conversions attribute the entire measured force to the nozzle and neglect the friction of the solid filament in the cold end. This work quantifies that contribution and its consequences for in situ rheometry. Extrusion forces were recorded for PET and PETG at three nozzle temperatures each, covering apparent shear rates of 77–2300 s −1 with a 0.4 mm nozzle, and a dedicated open‐bore reference isolated the friction force. Friction accounts for 52%–92% of the total force at the lowest feed speed and falls below 10% only above 4–5 mm/s, so that the speeds typical for perimeter printing coincide with friction fractions of up to 80%. Subtracting it changes the apparent viscosity by 35%–170% at the lowest equilibrated shear rates and also qualitatively: in the uncorrected data the decaying friction fraction masks the increase in flow resistance that the corrected data reveal. The corrected viscosity was compared with high‐pressure capillary rheometry using an adapter that mounts the identical nozzle on the laboratory instrument. With increasing shear rate the in situ curves approach isotherms of successively lower temperature, indicating that the effective melt temperature decreases as throughput increases.

title: No friction required: Self-locking in entangled assemblies of curved filaments
abstract: Filaments are incredible material building blocks that, when entangled together, form robust structures with remarkable adaptive mechanics, from stiff cables to stretchable knits. Basic questions about the mechanism that holds together such structures, especially assemblies like rope, without attractive physical or chemical bonds between constituents are among the oldest considered in materials science. Contradicting a long-standing picture that structural integrity of rope-like assemblies rely on a combination of external loading and inter-filament friction to prevent spontaneous detangling (e.g. fraying of a cut rope), we demonstrate that assemblies of intrinsically-curved filaments can achieve structural integrity purely from the competition of elastic forces that resist shape-change and (traction-free) repulsive forces that prevent overlap. abstract: ABSTRACT Nitinol (NiTi) stents are widely used for biliary decompression, but their biofluid‐exposed metallic surfaces remain susceptible to mechanical irritation, bacterial colonization, sludge deposition, and inflammation‐associated restenosis. The modified surface formed a continuous liquid‐infused architecture, exhibited water sliding angles <0.5°, and reduced adhesion under the tested conditions. SASLIPS decreased the coefficient of friction (COF) from 0.69 (NiTi) to 0.09 (SASLIPS), reduced biliary sludge accretion, inhibited 96.98% of E. coli adhesion and biofilm formation, and attenuated inflammatory responses, while preserving macroscopic thermally induced shape recovery. title: Three-Dimensional Thermomechanical Analysis of Radial Friction Welding of Dissimilar Copper-Aluminum Alloys: Finite Element Modelling and Experimental Validation
abstract: This study investigates radial friction welding of dissimilar AA2024 aluminum and Cu-DHP copper using a three-dimensional finite element model together with optical metallography, Vickers microhardness measurements, and thermocouple measurements. A coupled thermomechanical model was implemented in ANSYS Workbench 2023 R1 at 1 400 rpm and 30 MPa. The numerical solution predicts an asymmetric thermal field with a maximum of 750 °C at the Al-Cu interface, an equivalent plastic strain of 0.0177 mm/mm, and a maximum total displacement of 0.130 mm. The strain and displacement fields were interpreted together with the optical observations, which indicate localized thermomechanical modification and preferential material flow near the interface. The thermomechanically affected zone (TMAZ) reached approximately 157 HV. Direct comparison with thermocouple measurements and the measured aluminum-side TMAZ width supported the model for the directly comparable quantities. Microhardness provides complementary evidence of localized hardening but does not constitute direct strain measurement or phase identification. The model is useful for interpreting the thermomechanical response of AA2024/Cu-DHP radial friction welds, while the assumptions regarding friction and radiation, the absence of latent heat, and the absence of microstructural-kinetics modelling remain explicit limitations.

title: Development of surface modified Mg-2Gd-2Yb alloy through friction stir processing: corrosion behaviour and short-term anodic performance
abstract: This study investigates the influence of friction stir processing (FSP) on the microstructural evolution, corrosion behaviour and electrochemical performance of Mg–2Gd–2Yb alloy shows potential for further evaluation in short-duration cathodic-protection applications. The as-cast base material (BM) was processed using two FSP conditions: FSP02 (2 passes, 33 mm/min, 1400 rpm) and FSP04 (4 passes, 33 mm/min, 1400 rpm). FSP significantly refined the coarse-grain structure of the BM from approximately 808 µm to 8–10 µm, producing a homogeneous and defect-minimized microstructure. FSP02 exhibited the most effective grain refinement, while FSP04 showed slight grain coarsening due to cumulative heat input during multiple passes. Transmission electron microscopy revealed improved particle dispersion and strong particle matrix interactions in the processed specimens. Corrosion behaviour was evaluated under thermo-static (− 20 to 80 °C) and thermo-cyclic conditions. The BM exhibited severe localized corrosion characterized by pitting, cracking, and unstable corrosion product layers. In contrast, FSP specimens developed more uniform corrosion morphologies owing to refined grains and enhanced elemental distribution. At elevated temperatures, corrosion mechanisms shifted from chloride-assisted attack to the formation of protective MgO/Mg(OH) 2 -rich surface layers. title: Tribocharging of Granular Materials Dictated by Geometric and Thermoelectric Effects
abstract: Tribocharging of granular materials is a widespread phenomenon ranging from volcanic eruptions and dust storms to pharmaceutical processing, yet its underlying mechanism remains elusive. Recent thermoelectric models have provided a quantitative framework for triboelectric charge transfer, but they have difficulty accounting for charging between identical materials. In this Letter, we propose a theory of granular tribocharging based on the interplay between particle geometry and thermoelectric response. Collision-induced frictional heating produces a size-dependent temperature asymmetry between particles, generating a thermoelectric voltage that drives charge transfer. The sign of the Seebeck coefficient determines the charging polarity, while particle size and thermal properties set its magnitude. Our multi-collision theory explains the experimentally observed size- and material-dependent reversal of charging polarity, as in quartz and nylon.

abstract: Dealership showrooms are where a manufacturer’s brand promise is either turned into a booking or lost to a neighbouring dealer, yet published work on Indian passenger-vehicle retail rarely looks inside a single showroom. title: Mobility of dry granular flows over contrasting erodible bed materials in laboratory experiments
journal: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
abstract: Abstract. Debris-flow mobility responds sensitively to erosion and entrainment that exchange mass and momentum across the flow-bed interface. Yet, the mechanical controls that cause some debris flows to accelerate during erosion while others decelerate are insufficiently understood. Recent theory attributes this divergent behavior to inertial contrasts between the moving mass and the erodible bed, suggesting that incorporating inertially weaker, neutral, or stronger substrate into the flow enhances, maintains, or reduces flow mobility, respectively. Here, we conducted flume experiments and surface-based measurements to assess how the inertia of the erodible bed affects the flow kinematics, erosion, entrainment, and runout of dry granular single-phase debris flows. We systematically imposed inertial contrasts by releasing a quartz slide of constant solid density over erodible beds with lower, equal, and higher solid densities representing inertially weak, neutral, and strong scenarios, and compare these alongside a reference case without erosion. Each scenario was repeated for fine sand and a sand-gravel mixture. Our results reveal consistent behavior across both particle-size distributions. Debris flows over low-density beds exhibit higher apparent mean erosion rates, faster flow fronts before deposition, and longer runout lengths, whereas flows over equal- and high-density beds evolve similarly, with shallower erosion, slower flow fronts, and shorter, more compact deposits.

title: Wear-Driven Generative Modeling: A Conditional Framework for Three-Dimensional Shape Synthesis Through Progressive Material Removal
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Three-dimensional generative modeling commonly constructs object geometry by sampling learned distributions, denoising latent representations, predicting point sets, or optimizing continuous scene representations. However, many natural objects acquire their characteristic shapes through progressive material removal rather than direct construction. River pebbles, rounded mineral grains, and polished surfaces exemplify processes in which repeated contact, friction, and impact progressively modify local geometry. This paper proposes Wear-Driven Generative Modeling (WDGM), a framework for synthesizing three-dimensional shapes through a controlled sequence of surface-removal operations. Given an initial geometry, WDGM maintains a geometric state, a local material-state representation, and a history of environmental interactions. A conditional wear operator estimates spatially varying material removal from contact exposure, local geometry, material properties, and environmental conditions. The resulting geometry is updated while preserving non-negativity of removal, approximate mass consistency, and surface validity. A conditional controller selects the wear environment and process intensity to guide the evolving object toward target shape characteristics, such as roundness, volume, surface roughness, and aspect ratio. title: Effect of sub-critical fluid shear flow on granular bed strength
abstract: Interactions between fluids and granular materials are prevalent on the Earth's surface. In the case of fluid flow over a sediment bed, the fluid imparts a shear stress to the granular materials. When the applied shear stress is above a critical value, the grains become entrained in the fluid flow. Prior experimental studies have shown that granular beds subjected to a sub-critical fluid flow can strengthen in the same direction as the sub-critical flow. In contrast, granular beds can become weaker in the direction opposite to the sub-critical fluid flow. To investigate the grain-scale mechanisms that control directional strengthening and weakening, we perform discrete element method (DEM) simulations of granular beds subjected to model fluid flows in two (2D) and three (3D) dimensions with varied inter-particle static friction coefficients and conditioning flow speeds. In these studies, the sub-critical grain motion does not cause significant bed compaction. Instead, we find that the strength of a granular bed in a particular direction is highly correlated with the fraction of {\it surface} grains that can be dislodged by a fluid force applied in that direction. Further, the anisotropic bed strength only persists over a finite time scale that is set by the Shields number. We also show that inter-particle static friction is not required for bed strength anisotropy, but varying the friction affects the magnitude of the anisotropy. title: A modified triaxial test for characterising soil–structure interface behaviour
abstract: Abstract A modified triaxial test (MTT) was developed to investigate soil–structure interface (SSI) behaviour under controlled triaxial conditions. The modification integrates custom-fabricated material pieces and a specialised loading cap, enabling direct vertical shearing of the soil interface within a standard triaxial apparatus. A dedicated calibration procedure was implemented to ensure accurate determination of soil interface shear response. Comparison with the modified direct shear test (MDST) showed that the MTT produced interface friction angles comparable to those obtained from the MDST, with differences of only 0.6–4.6% for the peak friction angle and 0.1–5.5% for the residual friction angle across the investigated interface roughness conditions. The MTT results were considered potentially more representative because the proposed configuration promotes a more even mobilisation of interface shear resistance than the MDST, while also providing improved control of the stress state and boundary conditions within a triaxial testing environment. Complementary FLAC3D simulations were conducted to examine the spatial distribution of stresses along the interface, indicating that shear stresses are mobilised in a broadly uniform manner over the majority of the interface length. Taken together, the proposed MTT provides a reliable, practical, and more versatile alternative for characterising SSI behaviour.

title: Dynamics of flexible filaments in granular media
abstract: Interactions between flexible structures and their surrounding media underpin many forms of animal locomotion, from the flapping of wings in air to the undulating propulsion of tails and fins in water. However, the coupling between deformable bodies and granular materials, crucial for movement in sandy environments, remains comparatively understudied. The equations governing flexible structures in viscous fluids do not apply to granular media, where resistive forces depend on motion direction rather than speed.We provide the first experimental validation of a predictive theoretical framework for deformable-body dynamics in granular media. In this framework, the shape of the filament arises from a balance between the internal elastic and the anisotropic friction forces. We test the model using experiments in which a filament is actuated through prescribed angular oscillations at its head while fully immersed in a granular medium. Across a wide range of driving amplitudes and filament stiffnesses, we observe characteristic localization of deformation near the driven end, consistent with the highly dissipative, friction-dominated medium. abstract: The removal of adhesive dressings from skin is a contact-rich manipulation that remains largely manual despite its clinical importance and the high incidence of medi- cal adhesive-related skin injury (MARSI). This dissertation presents a model-based framework for robotic adhesive dressing removal by integrating manipulator identification, peeling mechanics, and interaction control on a simple four-degree-of-freedom robotic platform. title: Building an Interdisciplinary Additive Manufacturing Ecosystem: A Case Study of TUM.Additive
journal: European Conference on Management, Leadership and Governance (ECMLG)
abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) is an intrinsically interdisciplinary technology, spanning materials science, process and mechanical engineering, and design, with applications from construction and aerospace to medicine and the life sciences. Its industrial relevance depends on combining innovative process technologies with strong application potential, yet this is frequently constrained by fragmented expertise across materials, design, and application disciplines. Research entities such as universities tend to reproduce this fragmentation because resources, incentives, and reputation are organised around individual chairs, professorships and departments. This paper asks how an interdisciplinary AM ecosystem is built and coordinated within a university, and which mechanisms enable and constrain that process. We address the question through a single, revelatory case study of TUM.Additive, a mission network at the Technical University of Munich uniting thirty-five chairs and professorships from seven TUM schools and over one hundred researchers, spanning all seven DIN EN ISO/ASTM 52900 process categories and five material groups. We read the case through a triple helix lens, complemented by entrepreneurial ecosystem theory, and analyse it using the network's three coordination mechanisms: Connect, Collaborate, and Communicate. title: Mechanical behaviour of Norway spruce fractions in single pellet pressing and consequences for using juvenile wood and branches
abstract: Abstract The rising demand for wood fuel pellets and increasing competition for conventional raw materials have intensified interest in alternative forest‑derived feedstocks. In this study, pellets were produced from sawdust originating from four debarked fractions of a single Norway spruce ( Picea abies ) tree: heartwood, sapwood, juvenile wood, and branches. Branches differ chemically and morphologically from stem wood, and their use may influence both pelletizing energy requirements and pellet quality. Pellets were produced using single pellet press systems at moisture contents between 6 and 12% (wb), and energy inputs were quantified as compression ( W comp ), friction ( W fric ), and total ( W tot ) . Pellet quality was evaluated through measurements of solid density, hardness, and mechanical durability. Overall, pellet quality was comparable among the stem‑derived fractions; however, pellets produced from branch material showed markedly inferior properties, e.g., durability and hardness, when processed under conditions optimized for softwood. The branch-derived feedstock also exhibited pronounced differences in cell morphology and chemical composition relative to the stem wood fractions. In several respects, pelletizing branch material appears more similar to pellet production from hardwood than from softwood. The implications of these findings for the utilization of juvenile wood and branches are discussed and recommendations for the industry is presented.

abstract: Abstract Sustainable ground improvement aims to use industrial and agricultural byproducts. Rice husk ash (RHA), a high-silica agricultural waste, can act as a pozzolanic soil stabiliser, while basalt fibre mesh (a natural, high-strength geotextile) can reinforce soil. This study assesses the combined effect of RHA and basalt mesh on the strength of compacted soil. title: “It’s the Shit That Puts Bread on the Table”
abstract: Abstract This article examines the changing circulation of human waste in Copenhagen between 1800 and 1950, tracing how the movement of faeces, urine, and latrine matter shaped the city’s sanitary transformation. Drawing on more than 500 digitized life histories from the Copenhagen City Archives together with contributions from the journal Politivennen, it follows human waste through streets, courtyards, and apartments to show how changing infrastructures reorganized relations between bodies, labour, agriculture, and the urban environment. Approaching sanitation from below, the article foregrounds how Copenhageners experienced and negotiated everyday waste practices. The memoirs reveal that sanitary modernization was not a linear process of eliminating waste but, rather, one of continually reorganization. As sanitary infrastructures expanded, human waste was progressively displaced from public view, redistributing responsibility and environmental burdens across space. Leaks, overflows, and material frictions repeatedly disrupted emerging sanitary orders, exposing modernization as patchy and incomplete. Bringing together perspectives on urban metabolism, sanitary ordering, ruination, and ferality, the article contributes to an understanding of how modern urban life was materially and socially constituted through the uneven circulation, concealment, and redistribution of its own residues.

title: The Engagement Advantage of Interactive Flipbook Interfaces over Static PDFs: A Synthesis of Behavioral Metrics, Cognitive Mechanisms, and Client-Side Rendering Architectures (2024–2026)
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Static PDF documents remain the dominant format for catalogs, reports, training materials, and marketing assets, yet empirical engagement data consistently show large performance gaps relative to interactive page-flipping (“flipbook”) interfaces. This paper synthesizes cross-industry behavioral metrics (time-on-content, completion rates, mobile usability, share rates, click-through), cognitive and spatial-memory explanations for the page-turn effect, and a technical comparison of rendering architectures. Particular attention is given to privacy, latency, and accessibility differences between traditional cloud-based conversion pipelines and modern client-side (browser-local) engines that process documents entirely in memory using WebAssembly, PDF.js, and WebGL. Findings indicate that well-implemented flipbooks deliver 2–5× improvements on key engagement metrics while enabling richer analytics and reduced distribution friction. The analysis concludes with practical recommendations for researchers, publishers, and platform designers evaluating document formats in 2026.

title: Corporate Pension Risk-Taking in a Low Interest Rate Environment
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences
abstract: We examine how funding deficit pressures shape the risk-taking of U.S. corporate defined-benefit pension plans and how targeted regulatory relief can mitigate these incentives. Using the 2012 Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act reform, which temporarily eased funding pressure by revising discount rate calculations, we show that plans receiving greater relief significantly reduced their equity allocations and shifted toward safer assets. This derisking was most pronounced among active plans and those sponsored by more financially constrained firms. Our findings demonstrate that targeted regulatory relief can curb risk-taking incentives even without altering underlying economic conditions or financial reporting standards and shed light on the likely (and unlikely) frictions driving such behavior. title: Evaluation of Welding Techniques for Fabricating Corrosion-Resistant Marine Components
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The fabrication of corrosion-resistant marine components is essential for improving the durability, safety, and reliability of ships, offshore structures, and marine equipment exposed to aggressive seawater environments. This review evaluates welding techniques used in fabricating marine components, focusing on their influence on corrosion resistance, mechanical properties, weld quality, and fabrication cost. The welding processes examined include gas tungsten arc welding, gas metal arc welding, shielded metal arc welding, flux-cored arc welding, submerged arc welding, and friction stir welding. The review discusses commonly used marine materials, including carbon steel, stainless steel, duplex stainless steel, aluminium alloys, copper-nickel alloys, and nickel-based alloys. It also examines major corrosion mechanisms, such as pitting, crevice, galvanic, intergranular, and stress corrosion cracking. Furthermore, the effects of welding parameters, heat input, filler-metal selection, and microstructural changes on welded-joint performance are highlighted. Corrosion evaluation methods, including immersion testing, salt spray testing, potentiodynamic polarization, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, are discussed. title: Shear Behavior of the Recycled Concrete Aggregate–Geogrid Interface Under Various Particle Size Distributions: Experiment Investigation and Prediction
abstract: Geosynthetic materials provide effective reinforcement for recycled concrete aggregate (RCA), offering a promising approach to green and low-carbon transportation development. This study investigates the interfacial shear behavior of RCA–geogrid systems under varying particle sizes (G1, G2, G3, G4), normal stresses (50, 100, 150 kPa), and shear rates (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 mm/min). Prediction models for interfacial shear strength and deformation are proposed. Results indicate that the interface exhibits shear softening across different particle size distributions and normal stresses. RCA with well-graded particle size distributions (G1, G2, G3) showed higher peak shear strength and friction angle, along with smaller vertical displacements, compared to poorly graded RCA (G4). While shear rate had little influence on peak shear strength, it significantly affected vertical displacement. Furthermore, predictive formulas for interface shear strength and deformation were developed considering the curvature coefficient. Since shear strength is critical in determining RCA’s capacity to resist shear forces, these findings highlight its importance for ensuring structural integrity and enhancing its application in sustainable construction.

abstract: Soft variable‐stiffness actuators have emerged as a promising solution in soft robotics, combining high shape adaptability with load‐bearing capability. abstract: Purpose. Geometric and material nonlinearities, the dynamic nature of loading, and contact interaction between elements were taken into account. abstract: Three-dimensional generative modeling has increasingly explored representations such as point clouds, voxels, implicit surfaces, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, and diffusion-based models. However, the mechanisms used to produce a target geometry are often separated from the physical processes through which particulate structures emerge in the real world. Sand dunes, gravel piles, powder deposits, and granular slopes are formed through the coupled effects of gravity, particle collisions, friction, rolling, settling, and collective mechanical stability. abstract: Abstract Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency and irregular mechanical energy into electrical energy for self-powered sensors, wearable electronics, Internet-of-Things devices and distributed energy systems. abstract: This white paper determines the effect of tip engagement on the slip strength and consistency of AngleLock™ single and double self-tapping threaded inserts used as end connections on the 40 × 40 mm (40-6, M6) extruded aluminum profile. title: Effects of microwave irradiation using a household microwave oven on the physical properties of polyester fabric and its implications for dyeing
abstract: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) fibers require high-temperature and high-pressure dyeing with disperse dyes owing to their hydrophobic characteristics. This process poses challenges in terms of energy consumption and environmental impact. Microwave dyeing has attracted attention as a method for tackling these challenges. Microwaves can heat materials rapidly and uniformly, and this technology is expected to reduce the dyeing time and improve energy efficiency. abstract: This dissertation investigates the dynamics of current-driven magnetic skyrmions, topological solitons in magnetic materials with broken spatial inversion symmetry, for low-power spintronic applications like racetrack memory and multilevel data storage. Skyrmions’ small size and low driving current requirements make them promising information carriers. The skyrmion Hall angle, influenced by current and pinning, provides insights for ambient-condition devices. abstract: Laser hardening is normally applied in the solid-state regime, and the behaviour of chromium steels treated at a line energy high enough to melt the surface is far less documented. Here 40Cr steel (AISI 5140) was laser hardened at 3000 W and 5 mm/s (600 J/mm) with one, two and three passes and compared with the untreated state by roughness measurement, microhardness profiling, quantitative porosity analysis, X-ray diffraction, dry ball-on-disc sliding against a 100Cr6 ball (6 N, 3 cm/s, 200 m, n = 3) and abrasive testing to GOST 23.208-79. One pass produced a hard (530–590 HV) but porous remelted layer, with 6–9% porosity in the top 300 µm and a dislocation density of 1.6 × 1015 m−2. Repeated remelting reduced the porosity to below 1%, while the near-surface hardness fell to 280–310 HV, the dislocation density decreased four- to five-fold, and the hardened region extended to about 1300 µm, indicating tempering of the previously hardened material. After grinding and polishing, the specific wear rate of the steel in sliding fell significantly (p < 0.001) from 6.5 × 10−5 to 2.9, 4.3 and 1.7 × 10−5 mm3/(N·m), i.e., by 54, 34 and 74%, whereas the friction coefficient, 0.62–0.66, did not differ between the states. Under loose abrasive, the mass loss fell by 8.4, 25.5 and 14.3%. Three passes are recommended for sliding contacts and two passes for abrasive conditions; a single pass is not recommended because of the porosity of its remelted layer.
